title: Hoehne Wells: Depth, Yield and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Hoehne wells have a 55-foot median depth, but records range to 1,225 feet. See yields, costs, water levels and local risks.
h1: What to Know About Wells Near Hoehne, Colorado
intro_html:
Well records near Hoehne show generally shallow plains wells, but the local range is wide. Among permitted wells within five miles, the median reported depth is 55 feet, with the middle half between 42 and 100 feet. The deepest recorded well reaches 1,225 feet.

That spread matters when buying land. A nearby well is useful evidence, not a guarantee. Construction records, reported yields and water levels are incomplete, so a driller should review the specific lot, access, geology and intended use before giving a firm bid.

sections.heading: Hoehne well depth depends on the local ground
sections.html:
Most recorded wells near Hoehne are shallow: 74% are under 100 feet, while 15% fall between 100 and 300 feet. The middle half runs from 42 to 100 feet, which gives a reasonable starting range for a drilling conversation. It does not establish the depth on a particular parcel.

The local records also include deeper exceptions: 6% are between 300 and 600 feet, another 6% exceed 600 feet, and the deepest record is 1,225 feet. The mapped aquifer descriptions are mostly unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifer, with four wells in Pierre Shale and two in Dakota. Plains alluvium and sedimentary rock can change over short distances, so neighboring construction logs are worth reviewing before accepting a bid.

sections.heading: What a Hoehne well may produce
sections.html:
Only 15 wells in the records report a pump yield, so the yield statistics are a limited sample. Among those reports, the median is 14.0 gallons per minute, with the middle half from 9.5 to 15.0 gallons per minute. Forty-seven percent report 5 to 15 gallons per minute, and another 47% report more than 15 gallons per minute.

No reported well is under 1 gallon per minute. That is encouraging for household planning, but it is not a promise for a new hole. A well’s usable supply also depends on storage, pump sizing, recovery and the proposed domestic, stock or irrigation use. Confirm the permit conditions with Colorado DWR, especially if the property will support more than ordinary household use.

sections.heading: The Hoehne water table is shallow in the few records available
sections.html:
Only four wells report a static water level. Their median depth to water is 20 feet, and the middle half is 18 to 21 feet. Those measurements suggest shallow water in the wells that were tested, but the sample is too small to describe every part of the Hoehne area.

There is not enough reported water-level information here to establish a decade-by-decade declining or rising trend. Static level can vary with season, pumping and recent precipitation. Ask for the date and conditions of any water-level measurement, and have a driller compare the lot with nearby logs rather than treating the 20-foot median as a guaranteed drilling target.

sections.heading: Who has drilled around Hoehne, and how active the records are
sections.html:
The permit history includes 127 wells in the five-mile study area, with 87 recorded as constructed. Permits extend from the 1950s through the 2020s, and the newest permit year is 2025. Activity was highest in the 2000s, when 44 permits were issued, followed by 22 in the 1990s and 14 in the 1980s.

Boday Well Drilling, listed with Alex Boday, appears on 16 records. Sharpe Drilling Co, listed with Lyle M. Sharpe, appears on 12, and the same company listed with Russell Sharpe appears on 7. These records show local history, not current availability or a recommendation. Confirm licensing, insurance, scheduling and the scope of the written proposal before hiring.

sections.heading: Hoehne drilling cost starts with the depth estimate
sections.html:
For the alluvium and plains sedimentary rock described in the local cost model, a typical drilling rate is $35-$55 per foot. At the 55-foot median depth, the drilled hole works out to about $1,900-$3,000. That is only the hole, not a complete water system.

A finished well with pump, pressure tank, trenching and electrical is estimated at about $7,900-$15,000 at that median depth. A deeper hole, difficult access, casing and grouting requirements, rock conditions or longer utility runs can change the total. Ask each driller to separate drilling, casing, grout, pump equipment, trenching, electrical and testing so bids can be compared on the same basis.

sections.heading: Check water quality, dry-hole risk and the building plan
sections.html:
Environmental review deserves attention near Hoehne. Within about 10 miles, the mapping shows 10 PFAS sampling or contamination sites and 39 historic mine features. There are no EPA Superfund or cleanup sites in that mapped search. These facts do not determine water quality at a specific parcel, so test an existing well and discuss a new-well testing plan with the driller and laboratory.

Low yield is not the only concern. Confirm casing and grout details, septic setbacks, suitable drainfield ground, access for a rig and room for tanks and electrical equipment. Household wells are commonly permitted for exempt uses, but added uses may require different water rights or an augmentation plan in an over-appropriated basin. Review the permit before planning a home, livestock operation or irrigation system.

sections.heading: A practical purchase or build check for land near Hoehne
sections.html:
Before closing, collect the neighboring well permits and construction records, especially around El Moro and toward Trinidad. The local data include 88 wells with a reported total depth but only 15 with a reported pump yield, so do not assume every record answers the questions you need. A driller can use nearby depth, casing and yield information to narrow the uncertainty.

For a buildable lot, make the well, septic, driveway and electrical layout work together. Confirm rig access, possible trench lengths and the location of the septic system before buying. Get a written drilling allowance that reflects the 55-foot median but recognizes records as deep as 1,225 feet. Also verify the permit, intended use and water testing requirements with Colorado DWR.

faq.q: How deep are wells near Hoehne, Colorado?
faq.a: The median reported well depth within five miles of Hoehne is 55 feet, and the middle half runs from 42 to 100 feet. Seventy-four percent are under 100 feet. The records also include deeper wells: the deepest is 1,225 feet, so a nearby shallow well does not guarantee the same result on your parcel.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Hoehne?
faq.a: The local cost model uses $35-$55 per foot. At the 55-foot median depth, drilling the hole is estimated at $1,900-$3,000. A finished system with pump, tank, trenching and electrical is about $7,900-$15,000. Access, deeper drilling, casing, grouting and utility distance can change the final proposal.

faq.q: How much water do wells near Hoehne produce?
faq.a: Only 15 local records report a pump yield. In that limited sample, the median is 14.0 gallons per minute and the middle half is 9.5-15.0 gallons per minute. Forty-seven percent report 5-15 gallons per minute and 47% report more than 15. Treat these as local indicators, not a guarantee for a new well.

faq.q: Is well water near Hoehne safe to drink?
faq.a: The mapped area has 10 PFAS sampling or contamination sites and 39 historic mine features within about 10 miles, with no EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Those mapped facts cannot establish safety at a home. Test an existing well, or arrange appropriate testing for a new well, and review results with a qualified laboratory or water professional.

faq.q: Is the water table dropping near Hoehne?
faq.a: The records do not provide enough water-level information to establish a trend. Only four wells report static water levels. Their median depth to water is 20 feet, with the middle half from 18 to 21 feet. Seasonal conditions and pumping can affect readings, so compare dated measurements from nearby wells instead of assuming a regional decline.
